common_name: Corno di Toro Giallo Pepper (Yellow-Ripening Italian Bull's Horn Pepper)

planting.note: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost date and transplant only once nights stay reliably warm, since this strain needs a longer season than most bell peppers to fully color to yellow.

directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun once nights stay reliably above 55F, staking or caging plants since the long, heavy pods can bend lighter branches. Corno di Toro Giallo is the yellow-ripening strain of the classic Italian bull's horn frying pepper, maturing from green to a bright golden yellow rather than the red of the standard Rosso strain, though both share the same tapering, curved eight-inch pods and thin, sweet flesh prized for roasting. The pale color develops fully only with extra time on the plant, so gardeners wanting peak sweetness should let fruit ripen past the green stage rather than harvesting early for yield. Roast or grill whole until the skin blisters and slips off easily, then dress the silky flesh with olive oil and garlic in the Italian antipasto tradition.

common_name: Corno di Toro Rosso Pepper (Red-Ripening Italian Bull's Horn Pepper)

planting.note: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost date; ripens somewhat faster to red than the Giallo strain ripens to yellow, giving a slightly earlier full-color harvest.

directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after all danger of frost, spacing plants far enough apart for good airflow around the tall, productive stems. Corno di Toro Rosso is the traditional red-ripening strain of Italy's bull's horn frying pepper, its long, twisted, tapering pods turning from green to a deep brick-red as they mature and sweeten. The thin walls caramelize quickly under high heat, so roasting or charring over an open flame brings out a smoky sweetness that a thick-walled bell pepper cannot match. Harvest continually through summer to encourage further fruit set, picking some pods green for a milder flavor and letting others ripen fully red for the most intense sweetness.

common_name: Georgia Sweet Onion (Yellow Granex-Type Short-Day Sweet Onion)

planting.note: In the Deep South, start seed in fall for overwintered transplants or set out sets in late winter, since a short-day type that needs the shorter daylight of southern winters to trigger bulbing.

directions: Set transplants or sets 4 to 6 inches apart in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, keeping weeds down early since onions compete poorly with weeds while bulbs are sizing up. Georgia Sweet is a Yellow Granex-type short-day onion grown throughout the Vidalia region of southeast Georgia, where the area's naturally low-sulfur soils contribute to the same mild, sweet flavor that makes true Vidalia onions famous, even though only onions grown within the legally defined Vidalia district may carry that trademarked name. The flattened globe bulbs have thin, pale yellow skin and mild, juicy flesh best eaten fresh, since the low pungency that makes sweet onions so pleasant raw also shortens their storage life compared to pungent keeping onions. Reduce watering as tops begin to yellow and fall over, then cure bulbs in a warm, airy, shaded spot for one to two weeks before moving them to storage.

common_name: Halo Candy Hollyhock (Sugar-Pink Bicolor Single Hollyhock)

planting.note: Sow directly in spring, or start indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost for first-year bloom, in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun.

directions: Plant in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil, staking the tall flower spikes in exposed or windy sites where the top-heavy blooms can lean. Halo Candy is one of three named colors in Thompson and Morgan's Halo series, distinguished from its Halo Cerise and Halo Blush series-mates by sugar-pink petals surrounding a bold, contrasting deep-purple halo ring at the center of each large single flower. Like other Halo selections it forms a bushy clump of coarse, rugose foliage before sending up sturdy spikes of bloom from early to late summer, offering better branching and a longer bloom window than many single-spike heirloom hollyhock strains. Water at the base rather than overhead to limit the hollyhock rust that readily disfigures foliage in humid weather, and remove spent spikes to encourage continued flowering.

common_name: Halo Cerise Hollyhock (Cerise-Pink Bicolor Single Hollyhock)

planting.note: Sow directly in spring, or start indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost for first-year bloom, in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun.

directions: Site in full sun against a fence, wall, or the back of a border, where the tall spikes gain some shelter from wind and passersby can admire the flowers at eye level. Halo Cerise carries large, cerise-pink single flowers with a deep purple central halo, a more saturated pink-red than the softer sugar-pink of its Halo Candy series-mate, held on the same sturdy, well-branched spikes typical of the Halo line. The bushy clump of coarse, rounded foliage persists at the base through the growing season, sending up flowering stems from early to late summer that draw bees and other pollinators steadily. Deadhead spent spikes to prolong the bloom period, and divide or replant self-sown seedlings in fall if a larger stand of Halo-type hollyhocks is wanted the following year.

common_name: Halo Blush Hollyhock (White Bicolor Single Hollyhock)

planting.note: Sow directly in spring, or start indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost for first-year bloom, in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun.

directions: Plant in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil at the back of a cottage-style border, where the tall flowering spikes provide vertical structure behind lower-growing perennials. Halo Blush is the palest member of the Halo series, opening white with a striking fuchsia-red halo ringing a yellow center, a sharper contrast than the pink-on-purple pattern of its Halo Candy and Halo Cerise series-mates. Plants build a bushy rosette of rugose green foliage before sending up sturdy, well-branched spikes of large single flowers from early to late summer. Because hollyhock rust spreads readily in wet, still air, water at the soil line rather than overhead and give plants room for good air circulation.

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or divisions in spring or fall in lean, well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; this low, prostrate selection roots readily wherever creeping stems touch soil.

directions: Plant in lean, sharply drained, slightly alkaline soil in full sun, since this thyme rots quickly in heavy, wet ground over winter. Kurt was collected in Thracia by Kurt Reschke and introduced into cultivation by German nurseryman Werner Simon around 2000, and it forms a dense, ground-hugging mat of small, dark green, distinctly lemon-scented leaves that stays lower and more prostrate than the broader-leaved species type. Clusters of pink-purple flowers splashed with dark crimson appear in summer and draw bees steadily, while the lemon-flavored leaves and flowers can season fish and vegetable dishes much like common lemon thyme. Shear lightly after flowering to keep the mat tight and prevent the woody center from opening up, and use it between stepping stones or trailing over a wall where its low, spreading habit can be appreciated up close.

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or divisions in spring or fall in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; this vigorous, mounding selection tolerates poorer soil than most culinary herbs.

directions: Plant in lean, well-drained soil in full sun, where this vigorous, mounding thyme tolerates poor, rocky ground better than richer garden soil. Oregano-Scented is a broadleaf thyme selection prized for shiny, dark green leaves that carry a savory, oregano-like fragrance layered over the typical thyme aroma, distinguishing it from the plainer scent of common culinary thyme. Clusters of lilac flowers cover the mounded plant in midsummer and are a strong draw for honeybees and other pollinators. Use the leaves anywhere a recipe calls for either oregano or thyme, and shear lightly after bloom to keep the habit dense and encourage fresh growth for continued harvest.
